tone_statements.quote: Wilson (1974:148-50) gives an explication of tone contrasts in the North Binandere language Suena, based on the 43 pairs of words he found which appeared to differ only in tone. [...] There appears to be two phonemic tones present, and the contrast appears to lie in where and whether the higher pitch occurs; thus only one tone requires marking. The tone occurs on the first or second syllable and can only occur on the second syllable if the word is tri-syllabic or longer. This is very like a Japanese-style pitch accent system. [...] [fn. 8] The relationship between stress and tone in Suena has not been analysed.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement between the two sources: both (Wilson 1980 grammar, p. 11; Wilson & Wilson 1973/2008 dictionary, p. iii) describe Suena as having a two-way lexical tone contrast and neither mentions word stress. Neither source supports the catalog's penultimate-stress record (penultimate stress, source catalog-all-2026-09-12, which carries no quote): the record is not contradicted, because a tone language can also have stress, but nothing in these two primary SIL descriptions states any stress placement, and the dictionary's own tonal minimal pair (aménà vs ámenà) shows that the position of high tone is lexical, not fixed on the penult. The origin of the penult claim therefore still needs a source; it did not come from either work listed here.

audit.reasoning: Quote check: all three deciding passages (Wilson 1969 sec.3-3.2 pp.89-90; SIL OPD 2004 p.3; Wilson 1974 p.10) are present verbatim in the copies we hold at the stated places. Deciding source: a 1969 seven-page SIL phonology sketch by the language's only describer; its stress rule is one sentence ('Stress occurs on the penult of poly-syllabic noun stems'), explicitly preliminary, restricted to noun stems, with verbs 'yet to be studied' (1969) / 'more irregular' (OPD 2004), and the 169-pp 1974 grammar retreats to 'not fully analyzed as yet'. sources.quote: No stress statement. 'Zia and Suena share a common phonology, with the exception that Zia has five nasal vowels which Suena does not have, and Suena has two distinctive tones which Zia does not have. Since the practical orthography adopted for Suena does not symbolize tone, the Zia and Suena practical orthographies are identical...' Part I covers only word list, phoneme chart, Zia nasalization.
sources.locator: Part I.B 'Comparative chart of phonemes', p.15 (scanned/)

sources.citation: Wilson, Darryl & Lael Wilson (compilers). 1973 [retyped 1977, web ed. 2008]. Suena-English Dictionary and English-Suena Dictionary. Ukarumpa: SIL. 87 pp. (SIL Language & Culture Archives 31122; text)
sources.quote: No stress statement. Tone: 'It is still uncertain what degree of functional load tone carries. There are about 40 minimal tone pairs that have been found to date. They have been noted here, using the SIL system of ́ to mark high tone, ̄ to mark mid tone, and ` to mark low tone. Only high and mid seem to contrast, as low occurs only word final (except for one syllable words). e.g. aménà parrot / ámenà backside'. Tone is marked on the minimal-pair headwords (e.g. atárà), so the dictionary is raw material for testing where the pitch peak sits on nouns, but it makes no claim about stress.

sources.note: Per Smallhorn 2011:80, Ross categorises Suena as a pitch accent system (re-reading Wilson's tone pairs); relevant to whether our 'fixed penult stress + contrastive tone' coding should carry a pitch accent caution. Secondary (based on Wilson), so low priority.

tone.says: Secondhand via Smallhorn 2011 section 3.6: Ross (2005a:26) suggests the tonal behaviour of the TNG verb was lost early; categorises Suena as pitch accent; shows the main tonal area of New Guinea with pitch accent languages in adjacent clusters, 'descended from tone languages but.. fewer tonal neighbours' (p.25); Suena an outlier. Nothing Baruga-specific seen.
